content: 1. The consumption of lyophilized beef by children was associated with low critical improvements in height-for-age z-scores (HAZ), weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ), and head circumference-for-age z-scores (HCAZ), as assessed by Kreb et al. The mean differences (MD) were 1.1, 1.6, and 0.6 higher, respectively, indicating slight improvements. 2. Children consuming pork showed moderate critical improvements in HAZ (MD 1.9 higher), WHZ (MD 1.2 higher), HCAZ (MD 0.5 higher), height (MD 4.7 higher), weight (MD 1.4 higher), and head circumference (MD 0.6 higher). These findings suggest pork consumption may positively influence growth metrics. 3. The consumption of eggs by children was associated with low critical improvements in stunting (19 fewer cases per 1,000, ranging from 75 fewer to 292 more) and hemoglobin levels (MD 7.1 higher). However, the certainty of these findings was low due to methodological limitations. 4. Skimmed milk consumption in children resulted in moderate critical improvements in triceps skinfold thickness (MD 1.8 higher) and head circumference (MD 0.4 higher). These findings suggest potential benefits for body composition and growth. 5. Fish and concoction consumption in children showed moderate critical improvements in triceps skinfold thickness (MD 0.8 higher), head circumference (MD 3.2 higher), and hemoglobin levels (MD 0.2 higher). These findings indicate potential benefits for growth and nutritional status. 6. Caterpillar consumption in children was associated with very low critical improvements in stunting (42 fewer cases per 1,000, ranging from 163 fewer to 113 more), wasting (25 fewer cases per 1,000, ranging from 73 fewer to 106 more), weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ; MD 1.7 higher), HAZ (MD 5.5 higher), WHZ (MD 2.2 higher), and anemia (240 fewer cases per 1,000, ranging from 335 fewer to 95 fewer). However, the certainty of these findings was very low due to significant methodological concerns. 7. Cow milk consumption in children aged 0–12 months, as assessed by Thorsdottir et al., showed very low certainty of evidence for hemoglobin improvements. The study had serious limitations, including lack of sample size justification, confounders not being accounted for, and very broad confidence intervals. 8. A more varied animal-source food (ASF) diet compared to a less varied ASF diet in children aged 6–23 months was associated with low critical improvements in stunting (299 fewer cases per 1,000, ranging from 302 fewer to 299 fewer). However, the certainty of evidence was low due to methodological concerns, including selection bias and potential funding-related conflicts of interest. 9. Milk and milk product consumption in children aged 6–59 months, as assessed by Marinda et al., showed moderate critical improvements in stunting. The study was observational and non-comparative, with some concerns about sample representativeness and potential bias. 10. Methodological limitations across studies included issues such as lack of blinding, small sample sizes, inconsistent findings, and potential biases related to funding sources. These factors reduced the certainty and generalizability of the findings. 11. Specific concerns included differences in blood collection methods (venous vs. capillary), lack of randomization concealment, incomplete follow-up data due to participant relocation, and potential conflicts of interest in studies funded by organizations with vested interests in promoting specific foods. 12. Overall, while some animal-source foods showed potential benefits for growth and nutritional outcomes in children, the evidence was often limited by methodological weaknesses, reducing the reliability and applicability of the findings.
